                    II
   Cod. Ottobonianus 313, I'ol. 1287/
         (Considerably reduced)
                          INTRODUCTION.

Any editor who takes in hand to set forth a text of the
Gregorian Sacramentary may reasonably be expected, before
entering on the discussion of his manuscript authorities and of
the method he has followed in dealing with them, to give some
account of the purpose he has had in view, and to furnish some
excuse for adding to the number of texts already published.
He is perhaps more bound to do so if much of the material he
has used has already been employed, and the ground of his work
been already to some extent covered, by an earlier editor.
   It may be well therefore to say quite clearly that this volume
is not intended to be in any sense a complete or final edition of
the Gregorian Sacramentary. For such an edition the time has
certainly not yet come : a good deal of work will have to be
done before any fruitful attempt is possible : and this book is a
contribution to the preparatory work. The object I have had in
view is the reproduction, in a clear and convenient form, with
such accuracy as I can secure, of a text representing a definite
period, important both for the study of the religious history of
Western Christendom and for that of the formation and
development of the Sacramentary. The book does not claim,
and is not intended, to be more than an instrument for the study
of these subjects. I believe that, as such an instrument, it will be
useful, and I hope that it will be found trustworthy by those who
may employ it in time to come.
   It is right also to state here, for the information of members
of the Society, that the idea of the work was suggested by
Dr. Wickham Legg, the Chairman of the Council, by whose
generosity complete '' rotographic " copies of the texts of the
three manuscripts employed have been made available for m\'
use.^ Without this invaluable help it would have been

   The scholars who produced editions of the Gregorian Sacra-
mentary in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries — Pamelius,
Rocca and Menard^ — aimed in the first place at reproducing the
text of the earliest manuscripts which they could find. But they
seem also to have desired to make their published text as com-
       plete as possible, and therefore to exclude nothing which
appeared in other manuscripts accessible to them which bore the
same title, unless it could be set aside as being clearly of a date
after the days of St. Gregory. They were inclined, apparently,
to run the risk of including non-Gregorian matter, rather than to
exclude anything which seemed to have a claim to be treated as
an integral part of the Sacramentary. Thus Pamelius used as
his principal source a manuscript of the Chapter Library at
Cologne, which he believed to be of a date earlier than 833^ :
but he used also other manuscripts from Cologne, from Ghent
and from Utrecht. The account of his sources contained in the
preface to his work is very brief, and he does not succeed in
making it easy to understand the method which he followed, or
the relation of his printed text to the various sources, either by
his statements in the preface, or by the marginal and other notes
which accompany his text or are imbedded in it. But he marks
certain portions of his text by brackets, regarding them,
apparently, as added matter, either as being obviously of a date
later than the time of St. Gregory, or on the ground of their not
being found in the earliest of the manuscripts from which his
text was drawn.
   Rocca's text was derived from a Vatican manuscript of the
last years of the tenth century.^ Menard chose as the principal
source of his text a Corbie manuscript known as " Missale
Sancti Eligii."*   In this decision he was guided partly by a

   The first five pages of the Gregorianuni are written in an
ornate style in white (save for a few lines in gold) on a purple
ground, mainly in uncial script, but with occasional lines in square
capitals : the letters vary a good deal in size, and words are
awkwardly divided as though the scribe had failed to estimate
the space required for them. The last of the five pages, containing
the Preface and Sanctus, is entirely in uncial script. The body
of the book is in a bold and clear minuscule hand, the titles of
masses and prayers, and the rubrics, being for the most part in
uncials : rustic capitals are also used, but very sparingly. Words
left out by the original scribe and added by the contemporary
corrector in the margins are generally in small majuscule
characters : these are also used in a good many places by the
original scribe in abbreviations at the end of collects {e.g., PER
D N I X). The large initial letters of the prayers are frequently
ornamented in outline or otherwise slightly decorated : in two
cases (fol. I2i'z;. and fol. 17 $v.) the decoration takes the form of
dots surrounding the letter.
   In several places numbers are prefixed to the capitula. These
are not consecutive, but the numbers agree with one another,
reckoning the intervening capitula. They point to an archetype
in which the sections of the Gregorianuni were numbered
throughout. There is no musical notation in any part of the
text. The only punctuation mark of the original scribe seems
to be the simple point, which is not very freely used.
   The orthography of the scribe is not of a high standard : as
Mr. Bishop has remarked^, the text " abounds in solecisms and
grammatical errors," and there are also errors of transcription
due apparently to the carelessness of the scribe. The following
points in his usage are perhaps worthy of mention :—
      (i) The Sanctus is never written in a form extending
           beyond the third repetition of the word " Sanctus,"
           which is sometimes written thrice, sometimes once with
           the addition of the word " ter."
      (2) In the terminations of collects, the scribe appears to
           ignore the systematic variations which are commonly

beginning with that after Christmas and ending with Advent (ff. 2-24) ; and for a
small numljer of Saints' days (ff. 241-245) ; Confirmation (ff. 204-205). There are
also a few additional Masses, and a few Prefaces and Benedictions outside the series
mentioned above. The two series of Benedictions appear to be both by the same
hand, later than the series of Prefaces. The leaves from fol. 206 to fol. 221, and
those from fol. 222 to fol. 245, were probably successive additions to the volume, the
last pages of the second group being at first left blank, and afterwards utilized when
the Benedictions (ff. 2-24) were added at the beginning of the volume. For
information as to the script and gatherings of the later additions my thanks are due to
Monsieur Henri Omont.

   R {Codex Reginae 337) has 253 numbered leaves, arranged in
32 quires, all of which, except the sixth, were of eight leaves.
The last leaf of the last quire is wanting. The sixth quire
contains only six leaves, but the text is continuous, and there is
no reason to suspect that anything has been lost at this point.
   The first quire, which includes all the decorative writing of the
manuscript,- is by a different hand from the rest of the book.
The first two pages (" In nomine . . . celebratur") are in square
capitals, the third and fourth (" Hoc est in primis . . . Dignum
et iustum est ") in rustic capitals ; the next page and a half,
containing the Preface and Sanctus, are in uncials, which are
used also for the first line of " Te igitur." The V of **Vere
dignum " and the T of " Te igitur " are ornamental letters.
Throughout the manuscript uncials or rustic capitals are
employed for titles and rubrics. The rest of the writing is a fine
Carolingian minuscule, with plain capitals for the initial letters
of the prayers. There are few abbreviations, all of an ordinary
character, except the symbol     V, which, in the collection of

Prefaces, is used alternately with the more        usual symbol     of

   The manuscript has evidently been prepared with great care,
and the work of the first scribe has been revised and amended
by a correcting hand, the corrections being made by the erasure
and re-writing of the faulty words. The first scribe seems to
have had a tendency to omit syllables and sometimes whole
words^ ; and the correction has sometimes required the erasure
of more than one word in order to bring the correct reading into
the space available without writing anything between the lines,
or extending into the margin ; in a few cases, the writing of the
corrector does so extend ; but the words are always shown in
their proper order. Some of the work of correction appears to
have been done by the original scribe ; most of it by a hand
which bears a close resemblance to that of the writer of the first
quire ; a small amount, especially in the last portion of the
manuscript, by another hand, also apparently contemporary.
The spelling of the first hand is for the most part regular and
normal, save for the substitution of ^ (or even ae) for e, and
(more rarely) of e for ae. In the matter of the modification of
consonants in compound words, however, the scribe is rather
uncertain. Thus he writes {e.g.) both conpelle and compelle ; both
inpelle and impelle ; inininere, innninere and iininere ; adsiune
and assume ; adniitte and ammitte. Such forms as coinmitetur
for coviitetur (p. 84), aimnittamus for aniittaimis (p. 169), abtarida
for aptanda (p. 8), obtaiiit for optauit (p. 143), are perhaps due
to a mistaken application of a rule. The abbreviation krmy
 (= karisshni^ pp. 209, 211) may be derived from an abbreviation
 in which the final i was carried downwards below the line.
    There are very few later additions to the text, or alterations
 by later hands. One such addition is the Memento added to the
 Canon on fol. 6r., which is in a twelfth-century hand, of the type
 rather of a French charter-hand than of a book-hand : another is
 the pra}'er added on fol. 139^., which is perhaps of the tenth
 century : an alteration on fol. 957/. is also much later than the
 original hand. The names interlined at the ^r\^oi \}c\& Benedictio
 cerei must have been inserted between 858 and 872.^ In the
 Benedictio cerei there also occur a few signs of musical notation,
 which are apparently later additions.
    The punctuation marks are in many cases apparently added,
 either by the correctors or b)' a later hand. The signs most
 regularly employed are the simple point and the i In some of
 the longer forms, and especially in those which would, or might,

be sung in the manner of a preface, other signs are used. These
are the comma, marking a pause of the value of a semicolon or
colon, the semicolon, and the point followed b}' a comma. The
value of the semicolon appears to be intermediate between that
of the comma and the point and comma : but it appears possible
that the significance of these signs is musical rather than
grammatical.
   The Gregortanuni extends from fol. \r. to fol. 1397^. On the
last page a blank space was left, which is now filled by a prayer
in a later hand.^ The table of the contents of the supplement
begins (without ^ny praefathcnaila^ and without an)- heading) on
fol. 14O/-. and ends at the bottom of fol. 144;'. The numbered
sections begin on fol. 144^'. and extend to fol. 2297'., where a
blank space has been left before the title of the first of the series
of Prefaces, which appears at the foot of the page, the Preface
following on fol. 230;'. The series of Prefaces ends on fol. 245^
and is followed without break b\' " Incipiunt Benedictiones
Episcopales." The series of Benedictions fills the remaining
pages, and apparently extended at least to the leaf now wanting
at the end of the last quire.
   There seems to be no reason to doubt that the manuscript was
written in France ; but there is no indication of the actual place
of writing, or of the place where it was in use. The addition on
fol. 6r. may be said to give some evidence that it was in France
in the twelfth century : the earliest indication of ownership which
it contains shows that it was in France in the seventeenth. This
indication is found in the inscription on the first paper fly-leaf: —
        "Joan. Tarinus Regius eloquenti[ae] Professor"
to which is added rather lower on the page :—
                   " Is. heraldi curae credidit."
   Jean Tarin became Professor of Greek and Latin Eloquence
in the Royal College at Paris in 1629, and died in 1666. " Is.
Heraldus " is probably to be identified with Isaac Herauld, the
godson and namesake of Isaac Casaubon, who published at
Paris in 1650 some posthumous treatises of his father, Didier
Herauld, scholar and advocate. It was probably through Isaac
Herauld that the book was acquired for the collection of Queen
Christina of Sweden. Two notes in the handwriting of Isaac
Vossius, on fol. ir., show that the volume was in his hands in
1656, and was then numbered by him as "45 N. P.," that is,
No. 45 of those manuscripts in the queen's collection which were
classed as " Non Petaviani," having been acquired from some

the " Bibliotheca Alexandrina." It bears two press-marks,

to a belief that the manuscript had been lost.

   The entry relating to Lothair was probably added soon after
his death in 855 : " Hugo rex" is no doubt Hugh Capet, who
died in 996 : the abbot Hilduinus is no doubt the abbot of St.
Denis, who died, it is said, in 842. The entry referring to
Ragenoldus seems to be among the latest of the additions.
   This portion of the contents of the volume was examined by
the Bollandist Fathers Papebroch and Henschenius, who assigned
Bourges as the place of its origin. In this opinion they relied
solely on the entry, by the original hand, on Aug. 27th,
 " Bituricas dedicatio ecclesiae S. Sulpitii confessoris." Dom H.
 Ouentin, however, points out that on similar grounds other
 localities might be suggested, and attaches more importance to
 the indications which point to Paris or its neighbourhood as the
 place where the Martyrology was used.^ It is true that these
 are for the most part not by the first hand ; but they are
.sufficiently numerous to leave little doubt that the Martyrology,
 if not written at Paris, had come to that place, or to its immediate
 neighbourhood, soon after it was written. It was probably
 bound up with the Sacramentary at an early date : for the verso
 of fol. 6, originally left blank, has been filled with matter of the
 nature of additions to the Sacramentary, the first of which is
 apparently not much later than the Sacramentary itself^
    (ii.) The Sacramentary begins on fol. 7 recto and ends about
 the middle of the recto of fol. 213, with the inscription,
" Expliciunt Benedictiones. Amen." It originally consisted of
210 leaves, gathered in 27 quires, the first of which was of two
leaves only, the rest of eight leaves each. Three leaves are now
wanting in the twentieth quire, between fol. 156 and fol. 157 : the
nineteenth quire has nine leaves, fol. 147 being an inserted leaf,
most of the contents of which are by later hands.
   The title and the outline of the order of the Mass, with the

highly ornamented monogram of Vere digmini. There is no
ornament in the rest of the manuscript. The initial letter of Te

prayers are also plain throughout. The body of the manuscript
is written in a good minuscule hand of the ninth century, which

very clear distinction in value, so far as the sense is concerned.
They occur, for the most part, in the prefaces and in other forms
where they may be supposed to have a musical significance.

   On the question at what place the Sacramentan- was written
or used its text yields one piece of evidence. In the Libera
after the Lord's Praver at the end of the Canon, the names of
SS. Denis, Rusticus, Eleutherius and Chlodoald are added after
those of SS. Peter and Paul and St. Andrew.^ This addition
certainly suggests the neighbourhood of Paris : the mention of
St. Chlodoald seemed to the Benedictine editors of St. Gregory
to be decisive in favour of the church of St. Cloud at Nogent.
But it does not seem certain that St. Cloud might not, even at
Paris itself, have been commemorated in this \\ay : and the
evidence afforded b}' some of the names which appear on
ff. 109-11 seems rather to suggest that when those names were
written the book was in use in Paris.
   The earliest entries on these pages seem to be those on
fol. iiir., where a beginning appears to have been made by two
lists, one of bishops, the other of secular princes, in two columns.
The heading " Nomina defunctorum," which now stands almost
directly above the first of these lists, probably refers to both, and
perhaps to all the names on the page. But it seems to have
been written later than the first names in the lists, and though it
was probably an accurate description of the lists at the time
when it was written, it may be that the lists were original!}- lists
of benefactors, to which names were added even during the lives
of the persons concerned.-
   The first list begins with the names of " Domnus Inchadus
episcopus, Ercanradus episcopus, Ermbertus episcopus, Guntbal-

Hilduinus abba." The second column begins with " Carolus
imperator, Hludouuicus imperator, Pippinus rex " ; then a space
has been left before the names of" Stephanus comes, Amaltrudis."
A third column begins, rather further to the right, with the
following names, in a somewhat later hand : " Carolus imperator,

   " Domnus Inchadus episcopus" is no doubt the bishop of Paris
of that name whose death is said to have occurred in 831. He
was a benefactor of the chapter of Paris. It is noticeable that
his is the only name of a bishop appearing in these pages to
which the title " Domnus " is prefixed : its presence seems to
suggest that, if he was not actually bishop at the time when his
name was written, the interval since his death had not been
long. "■ Ercanradus episcopus " may be either Ercanradus I.
{pb. c. 795), who is said to have first constituted the chapter^ or
Ercanradus II., the immediate successor of Inchadus, who is said
to have held the see from 831 to about 857. The other bishops
whose names follow do not seem to have been bishops of Paris :
they may be identified, however, with occupants of various other
sees in North France before 850.
   The second column begins with Charles the Great, his son
Louis, and his grandson Pepin of Aquitaine. " Stephanus
comes " and Amaltrudis are Stephen, Count of Paris, and his
wife, who made a joint grant to the church of Paris in 81 1.^ The
name of Lothair may have been added after the emperor's death
in 855 : it had probably already filled the space left after Pepin's
name when the name of Charles the Bald came to be added ;
this was placed at the head of a new column because there was
not room for it among the names of his kindred in the second
column. Judith and Hirmingardis may possibly be the wives
of Louis I., but if they are so, they are placed out of order. It
is perhaps more likely that Judith is the daughter of Charles the
Bald, who became, in 836, the wife of the English King Ethel-
wulf, and Hirmingardis the daughter of Louis II., whose husband
Boso became King of Provence in 879.
   Another list of names, on fol. iioz^., also supplies evidence
of the connexion of the manuscript with Paris. It is headed
"Nomina canonicorum Parisiacens," and begins with "Ercanradus
episcopus " : the last name but one in the column is " Fulradus
episcopus." The list, therefore, was probably begun in the time
of Ercanradus II. (between 831 and 857) and carried on till the
time of Fulradus {c. 922-6). Among the names of bishops
which appear in the less systematically ordered entries there are
at any rate four which seem to be those of bishops of Paris, the
latest being Elisiardus {c. 987-9) or Raynaldus.-
    ^ Gallia Christiana torn. vii. col. 30 (ed. 1744).                                \
    '■^ Raynaldus may be the predecessor of Elisiardus, or a later Raynaldus {c. 992-
1016). The names of Robert II. and his wife Constancia {c. 999-1031) are the lates
which can be certainly identified among the additions to the original entries.

   On the whole, it may be said that the names of the saints
which appear in the Libera are evidence that the Sacramentary
was written for some church in or near Paris, while the names
recorded for commemoration are evidence that it was in use
at the cathedral church of Paris soon after it was written, and
probably before 850. There seems to be no evidence which
points clearly to any other place as that of its origin.^
   The codex had apparently already passed in the sixteenth
century into the hands of a private owner : for a note in the
handwriting of that period, on the verso of the fly-leaf, states
that

      " Ce liure et a Ih. gautier (?) qui le trouvara si le porte en
           son otel a la Rue de Quacot et il aura bon vin etc."
Later, it was in the collection of Paul Petau, and was one of
the manuscripts purchased from that collection by Vossius for
the Queen of Sweden, and acquired with her other manuscripts
by Cardinal Ottoboni. When, as Alexander VIII., he formed
the " Bibliotheca Alexandrina," this volume was not included in
that collection, but was one of those reserved for the Pope's
private library. It was purchased, with the rest of that collection,
from the Ottoboni family by Benedict XIV., and by him
bestowed upon the Vatican Library. Its number in the Queen
of Sweden's collection was 1275. Vezzosi refers to it as
Number 2 of the Ottoboni collection, soon after that collection
became part of the Vatican Library-, and this mark appears
on one of the paper fly-leaves. Giorgi, writing rather earlier,
refers to it as " Sacramentarium Gregorianum in Bibliotheca
Ottoboniana, olim Reginae Svecorum num. 1275, nunc n. 327."^
Of this last numeration the manuscript now bears no trace ; but
its present binding is of the time of Pius IX.

there are differences, not indeed of great importance, but not

illustrate the development of that type of Sacramentary which
was produced under Charles the Great for use in his Prankish
dominions, and which throughout the ninth century continued to
be the normal and recognized type in that part of Europe.
In C we have an example of the earliest stage in the process ;
it is an instance, the only one, probabl}', now traceable, of the
Prankish use of the Gregorian " libellus sacramentorum " derived
from the Gregorianum sent by Hadrian, by itself, and apart from
the supplement.^ The other two manuscripts, R and O, exemp-
     lify, in the combination of the Gregorimiiivi with the numbered
sections of the supplement, the most important and permanent
results of Alcuin's work on the Sacramentary. With regard to
the matter which follows the numbered sections, it is, perhaps,
more doubtful whether either manuscript illustrates Alcuin's
work, or which of them seems more likely to do so. But the
corresponding portion of the supplement, as we have seen, was
probabl}' regarded as secondar}', both in importance and in
authorit}', to that in respect of which R and O are in substantial
agreement.

Sacramentaries enumerated by Ebner as representative of the

significance can hardly be of any importance at all.

O and R proceed on different lines. The collection of Prefaces
and Benedictions which is provided in R has been framed on the
principle of supplying a small number of forms for particular
days, and groups of forms for particular seasons, for festivals of
saints, for Sundays, and for special purposes. The number of
Prefaces allotted to particular days is at the most fourteen, that of
Benedictions so allotted not more than twelve.^ In O the col-
         lection contains a very much larger number of forms, and these
are for the most part assigned to particular days : every Sunday,,
for example, has its own Preface. Most of the forms contained
in R are found also in O ; but the two collections seem to be
independent of each other, though doubtless much of their
material has been derived directly or indirectly from the same
source.
   The series of Prefaces in O is preceded by a short introductory
heading, in which the collection which follows seems to be dis-
                 tinguished from the sections '' studiose perscripta " which precede
it.^ This paragraph appears also in several manuscripts of the
same group to which O belongs, with little variation. But the
collection of Prefaces to which it is prefixed is possibly not the
same in all cases : the omission or addition of Prefaces in such a
series might be varied a good deal according to local require-
        ments : and it may perhaps appear from an examination of the
kindred books that other divergences are to be found within the
group as great as that which exists between O and R.
   It cannot be regarded as certain that either O or R contains
the same series of Prefaces and Benedictions which was
originally associated with the numbered sections of the supple-
       ment : and in the case of O there are some points which seem
to give grounds for the opinion that its collection was formed
independently of the G^^egorianMin and of Alcuin's supplement.
The method of reckoning the Sundays after Pentecost is different :
in the numbered sections, as we have seen, O reckons them from
the Octave : its Prefaces are reckoned from Whitsunday, and
their number is greater than the number of masses provided in
the supplement for these Sundays. There are three Prefaces
placed before that for the third Sunday " post octavas Paschae ""

Benedictions of R contain a smaller proportion of forms common
to the series of O ; and those of O contain a smaller proportion
of forms assigned to particular days. There are few Benedictions
in either series for festivals of particular saints.^
    The method which I have thought it best to follow in the
 present edition may be very briefly described. I have taken the
 text of the Gregorimmin and of the numbered sections of the
 supplement from R, indicating in footnotes the variant readings
 of C and O, and the additions which O makes to the text of R,
 but inserting between the Gregoyianuvi and the supplement the
praefatiuncula as it appears in O. The Prefaces and Benedictions
 of both R and O have been printed in full. The cues from the
 Antiphonary which appear in the margins of O are given in a
 separate series of footnotes. A few masses added by later
 hands in the margins of O, and the additional matter which
 appears on the page facing the title of that manuscript, are
 added in the Appendix.
    In making choice of R as the principal authority for the text
 I have been guided mainly by reasons of convenience. The
 selection of either of the other manuscripts would have involved
 a large increase in the amount of footnotes, since the text of C
 would have required much correction, and that of O many
 indications of corrections made in the manuscript itself. The
 text of R has also undergone a good deal of correction : but the
 corrections which have been made in it are, I believe, except in
 a very small number of places, not of the nature of alterations :
 and it has been possible to indicate the fact that corrections have
 been made without multiplying footnotes. For this purpose a
 sign has been employed in the text, where words which have
 been in whole or in part re-written are marked by small crotchets
^ ^ above the line at the beginning and end of the correction,
 save in cases where a footnote has been required for some other
 reason.
    In printing the text I have followed in all cases the spelling
 of the manuscript, adopting in the portions taken from O the
spelling of the first hand, even where this has been altered, if it
can still be clearly made out. Abbreviated words have been
expanded in accordance, so far as may be, with the ordinary spell-
      ing of the scribe. In dates, when it is uncertain how the scribe

would have expanded an abbreviated word, either because he
never expands it, or because his practice varies, I have used the
correct form of the word, giving him the benefit of the doubt.
   With regard to punctuation, I have followed as far as ma}' be
what now appears in the manuscripts, with the following excep-
         tions. Ihave conformed to modern usage by adding a full stop
at the end of forms, although the scribes generally omit this
sign ; and I have made uniform the varying use of a point in
connexion with numerals. In the portions of the text for which
O is the source, I have not always found it possible to decide,
in the combinations of point and virgule (other than :! and ;)
whether the scribe intended his virgule to surmount or to follow
the point, and it seemed best to employ uniformly for these
combinations the sign .,
   In indicating the variants of C and O I have not, as a rule,
taken account of mere variations of spelling ; nor have I always
noted ungrammatical variants, where no doubt can arise as to
the true reading. But otherwise I have thought it best to err on
the side of noting rather than of omitting even ver}' unimportant
differences.
   In the notes which give the cues from the Antiphonary as they
appear in O, round brackets indicate that what is enclosed in
them has now disappeared, through the operations of the binder :
square brackets indicate an addition or substitution by a later
hand : angular brackets indicate that words or letters omitted have
been supplied. The same significance belongs to round brackets
in forms contained in the footnotes ; and angular brackets,
wherever they occur, indicate that the words or letters enclosed
do not appear in the manuscript.

suggestions to various helpers, and in particular to the Rev. H. M.
Bannister and to those who aided him in his enquiries on my
behalf in the Vatican Library on many points of detail, to
Mr. Edmund Bishop, to M. Henri Omont, and, as on previous
occasions, to the Chairman and the Treasurer of the Henry
Bradshaw Society.

   Hucusque praecedens sacramentorum [Cod. Ott. 313. fo. 103
libellus a beato papa gregorio constat esse editus . exceptis his
quae in eodem in natiuitate uel assumptione beatae mariae .
praecipue uero in quadragesima uirgulis antepositis . lectoris in-
uenerit iugulata sollertia. Nam sicut quorundam relatu didicimus
domnus apostolicus in eisdem diebus ab stationibus penitus
uacat . eo quod ceteris septiman^ feriis stationibus uacando fati-
gatus . eisdem requiescat diebus. Ob id scilicet ut tumultuatione
populari carens . et elemosynis pauperibus distribuere . et negotia
exteriora liberius ualeat disponere. ]\Iissam uero praetitulatam in
natale eiusdem beati gregorii . uirgulis antepositis iugulatam a
predecessoribus^ eius causa amoris immouenerationis suae eidem
suo operi non dubium est esse interpositam. Praefatus sane
sacramentorum libellus . licet a plerisque scriptorum uitio depra-
uante . qui non ut ab auctore suo est editus haberetur pro captu
tamen ingenii ob multorum utilitatem ^studii nostri [fo. 1031^
fuit artis stilo corrigere., Quern cum prudens lector studiose
perlegerit : uerum nos dicere ilico comprobabit . nisi iterum
scriptorum uitio deprauetur. Sed quia sunt et alia quaedam qui-
bus necessario sancta utitur ecclesia . quae idem pater ab aliis
iam edita esse inspiciens . praetermisit., Idcirco opere pretium
duximus ea uelut flores pratorum uernantes carpere et in unum
congerere . atque correcta et emendata . suisque capitulis prae-
notata . in huius corpore codicis seorsum ponere . ut in hoc opere
cuncta inueniret lectoris industria . quaecumque nostris tempori-
bus necessaria esse perspeximus . quamquam pluriora etiam in
aliis sacramentorum libellis inuenissemus inserta. Hanc uero
discretionis gratia praefatiunculam in medio collocauimus . ut
alterius finis . alterius quoque exordium esset libelli., Ita uidelicet
ut hinc inde ordinabiliter eisdem positis libellis nouerit quisque
quae a beato gregorio quaeue sint ab aliis edita patribus . et
